summary: Defines XML formats for lists of resources, such as users, that a single URI can stand for. For instance, when a SIP SUBSCRIBE targets a list service, the server can expand the list and subscribe to each member.

plainLanguage.summary: A SIP address can name a service rather than a person, such as a list of friends whose presence you want to follow. This document defines the XML files that hold those lists and that tie a service address to one, so the server can subscribe to every member for you.

questions: what is a sip resource list
what is an rls services document
how does a resource list server expand a list
subtitle: Two XML formats for naming groups of users and for attaching a SIP service URI to such a group.

tldr.problem: In SIP, a service such as a presence list or a conference is named by a single URI, but the service needs a list of users to act on, and that list is useful even without any service attached to it.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines two XML document formats: a resource lists document holding named lists of resources, and an RLS services document that binds a service URI to a list and to the set of event packages it accepts. Both can be managed with XCAP.
tldr.outcome: A client can keep a shared, hierarchical list of users that other applications reuse, and a resource list server can expand a list, resolve its references and subscribe to every member on behalf of the subscriber.

today: RFC 4826 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines two XCAP application usages and registers the namespaces, schemas and media types that go with them, and the document itself points to the Presence Authorization Rules and the Resource List Server documents for the parts it does not cover.

sections.title: Services Named by a URI
sections.content:
SIP defines the SIP URI as any resource to which a SIP request can be generated for the purposes of establishing some form of communications operation. These URIs can represent users, for example sip:joe@example.com. The SIP URI can also represent a service, such as voicemail, conferencing or a presence list. A common pattern across such SIP services is that the service is defined and associated with a URI, and to operate, that service needs to make use of a list of users, or more generally a list of resources. When a SIP request is sent to the service URI, the server providing the service reads that list and then performs some kind of operation against each resource on the list.

One important example is a presence list service, which allows a client to generate a SIP SUBSCRIBE request to ask for presence information for a list of users. The presence list server obtains the presence for the users on the list and provides it back to the client. A presence list server is a specific case of a resource list server (RLS), which allows a client to generate a SIP SUBSCRIBE request to ask for notifications of SIP events for a list of resources. Another example is an instant conference service: if a client sends a SIP INVITE request to the URI representing the conference service, the conference server creates a conference call containing the client and the associated group of users.

It is very useful for a user of these systems to define the groups of users or resources, generally called a resource list, separately from the services that access those resource lists. There are uses for resource lists even with no associated network-based service: rather than use a presence list service, a client might generate individual SUBSCRIBE requests to obtain the presence of each user in a locally stored presence list, which needs a format for storing the list on disk. The user might also wish to share the list with friends and email it to them, which again requires a standardized format.

The document therefore defines two XML document formats: the first represents resource lists, independent of any particular service, and the second defines service URIs for an RLS and associates a resource list with the service URI. It also defines an XCAP application usage for managing each of the two documents.
sections.plainLanguage: A service address like a conference room or a friends list is a SIP address. Behind it sits a list of people. Keeping that list in its own file means the same list can feed several services and can be shared by email.

sections.title: The Resource Lists Document
sections.content:
A resource lists document is an XML document that MUST be well-formed and MUST be valid according to schemas, including extension schemas, available to the validator. Resource lists documents MUST be based on XML 1.0 and MUST be encoded using UTF-8. The namespace URI for the elements defined by this specification is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:resource-lists.

The document has the resource-lists element as its root, with no attributes. Its content is a sequence of zero or more list elements, each of which defines a single resource list. A list element can contain an optional name attribute, which is a handle for the list and, when present, MUST be unique amongst all other list elements within the same parent. A list element is composed of an optional display name, a sequence of zero or more elements each of which may be an entry, a list, an entry-ref or an external element, followed by any number of elements from other namespaces for extensibility. Because a list element can contain other list elements, a resource list can be hierarchically structured, and the display name gives a human-friendly name to each level of the hierarchy.

The entry element describes a single resource, defined by a URI, that is part of the list. It has a single mandatory attribute, uri, equal to the URI used to access the resource. The format itself does not constrain the type of URI that can be used, though the service making use of the list may require specific URI schemes: RLS services require URIs representing subscribeable resources, which includes the SIP and pres URIs. The uri attribute MUST be unique amongst all other uri attributes in entry elements within the same parent, determined by case-sensitive string comparisons. The entry element contains a sequence of elements providing information about the entry; only one such element is defined at this time, which is display-name, a UTF-8-encoded string meant for consumption by a human user. Unlike the name attribute, the display name has no uniqueness requirements, and it can carry the xml:lang attribute giving its language. The entry element can also contain elements from other namespaces, to support information such as a phone number or postal address.

The entry-ref element allows an entry to be included by reference rather than by value. It is only meaningful when the document was obtained through XCAP, in which case the referenced entry has to exist within the same XCAP root. It has a single mandatory attribute, ref, which MUST be unique amongst all other ref attributes in entry-ref elements within the same parent, by case-sensitive string comparison. The content of the ref attribute is a relative HTTP URI: it MUST be a relative path reference where the base URI is the XCAP root URI of the document in which the entry-ref appears, and if resolved into an absolute URI according to the procedures in RFC 3986, it MUST resolve to an entry element within a resource-lists document. Because the relative URI must be a relative path URI, the slash will never be the first character in the content of a ref attribute, and since the content is a valid HTTP URI it must be percent-encoded within the XML document.

The external element is similar to entry-ref, but it refers to an entire list and allows that list to be present on another server. It has a single mandatory attribute, anchor, which specifies the external list by means of an absolute HTTP URI and MUST be unique amongst all other anchor attributes in external elements within the same parent. The anchor value MUST identify an XCAP resource, and in particular it MUST represent a list element within a resource lists document, and it must be percent-encoded.

For both entry-ref and external, the responsibility of resolving the references falls on the entity making use of the document. With XCAP, that means the XCAP client. If the client is a PC-based application using the resource-lists document as a presence list, the references would likely be resolved on explicit request by the user, though they can be resolved at any time. If the client is an RLS itself, the references would be resolved when the RLS receives a SUBSCRIBE request for an RLS service associated with a resource list containing one of these references. An XCAP server defined by this specification will not attempt to resolve the references before returning the document to the client.
sections.plainLanguage: The document holds named lists. A list can contain people, other lists, pointers to an entry stored elsewhere, or pointers to a whole list on another server. The two kinds of pointer are the only ones that need looking up before use.

sections.title: The RLS Services Document
sections.content:
An RLS services document is used to define URIs that represent services provided by a Resource List Server. It is an XML document that MUST be well-formed and MUST be valid according to schemas, including extension schemas, available to the validator. RLS services documents MUST be based on XML 1.0 and MUST be encoded using UTF-8. The namespace URI for the elements defined by this specification is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:rls-services.

The root element of an rls-services document is rls-services, which contains a sequence of service elements, each defining a service available at an RLS. Each service element has a single mandatory attribute, uri, which defines the resource associated with the service: if a client subscribes to that URI, it obtains the service defined by the corresponding service element.

The service element contains child elements that define the service. For an RLS service very little definition is needed: the resource list to which the server will perform virtual subscriptions, and the set of event packages the service supports. The list can be conveyed in one of two ways: a resource-list element points to a list element in a resource-lists document, or a list element includes the resource list directly. The supported packages are contained in the packages element, and the packages element is optional; when it is absent, the RLS service will accept subscriptions for any event package.

By including the contents of the resource list directly, a user can create lists and add members to them with a single XCAP operation. The resulting list becomes hidden within the RLS service definition and is not usable by other application usages. The resource-list element exists as an alternative for exactly that reason: it can reference a list element in a resource-lists document, and since the list is separated from the service definition, it can be easily reused by other application usages.

The resource-list element contains a URI. It is only meaningful when the document was obtained through XCAP. The URI MUST be an absolute HTTP URI representing an XCAP element resource, and its XCAP root MUST be the same as the XCAP root of the RLS services document. When the document is present in a user's home directory, the HTTP URI must exist underneath that user's home directory in the resource-lists application usage; when it is in the global directory, the HTTP URI must exist underneath any user's home directory. In either case the element referenced by the URI MUST be a list element within a resource-lists document, and all of these constraints except that last referential integrity one are enforced by the XCAP server.
sections.plainLanguage: The services document is a list of service addresses. Each one points at a group of people, either by naming a group stored elsewhere or by carrying the group inline. Naming it elsewhere keeps the group reusable.

sections.title: How a Server Expands a List
sections.content:
When an RLS receives a SUBSCRIBE request for a URI present in the Request URI, it obtains the service element whose uri attribute matches, based on URI equality, the URI in the request. The document makes no normative statement on how this might be accomplished. One possible approach: the RLS canonicalizes the Request URI, then performs an XCAP GET operation against the URI formed by combining the XCAP root with the document selector of the global index with a node selector of the form rls-services/service[@uri=<canonical-uri>]. If the response is a 200 OK, it contains the service definition for that URI.

Once the service element has been obtained, it is examined. If the packages element is present and the event package in the SUBSCRIBE request is not among those listed in the package elements within packages, the request MUST be rejected with a 489 (Bad Event) response code. Otherwise it SHOULD be processed. The next step is to authorize that the client is allowed to subscribe to the resource, which can be done using the data defined in the Presence Authorization Rules document. Assuming the subscriber is authorized, the subscription is processed according to the procedures defined for the RLS, which requires the RLS to compute a flat list of URIs to subscribe to.

If the service element had a list element, it is extracted; if it had a resource-list element, its URI content is dereferenced and the result should be a list element, and if it is not the request SHOULD be rejected with a 502 (Bad Gateway). At that point the RLS has a list element and must obtain a flat list of URIs from it by traversing the tree of elements rooted in it. Before traversal the RLS initializes two lists, the flat list that will hold the URIs after traversal and the traversed list of HTTP URIs in external elements that have already been visited, both initially empty. The server may use any traversal ordering, such as depth-first or breadth-first. The processing at each element depends on its name.

An entry element contributes the URI in its uri attribute to the flat list if it is not already present, based on case-sensitive string equality, and the URI scheme must represent one that can be used to service subscriptions, such as SIP and pres. An entry-ref element has its relative path reference resolved into an absolute URI using the procedures in Section 5.2 of RFC 3986, with the XCAP root of the RLS services document as the base URI, and that absolute URI is dereferenced; if the result is not a 200 OK containing an entry element the request SHOULD be rejected with a 502 (Bad Gateway), and otherwise the returned entry element is processed as before. An external element has its anchor URI examined: if the URI is on the traversed list, the server MUST cease traversing the tree and SHOULD reject the request with a 502 (Bad Gateway); if it is not, the server adds the URI to the traversed list and dereferences it, and if the result is not a 200 OK containing a list element the request SHOULD be rejected with a 502 (Bad Gateway). Otherwise the RLS replaces the external element in its local copy of the tree with the list element that was returned, and traversal continues. Because the external element is used to construct the tree dynamically, recursive evaluation of references is possible, and the traversed list prevents it.

Once the tree has been traversed, the RLS can create virtual subscriptions to each URI in the flat list. When an entry-ref or external element contains a reference that cannot be resolved, failing the request is a SHOULD-level requirement. In some cases an RLS may provide better service by creating virtual subscriptions to the URIs in the flat list that could be obtained, omitting those that could not, and only in those cases should the SHOULD be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The server walks the list, following any pointers it meets and collecting the addresses it finds. A record of the pointers already followed stops one list from pointing back at itself and looping forever.

sections.title: Making URIs Comparable
sections.content:
Frequently, an XCAP client will wish to insert or remove an entry, entry-ref or external element from a document without having a cached copy of that document. In such a case, the uri attribute of the entry element, the ref attribute of the entry-ref element or the anchor attribute of the external element is used as an index to select the element to operate upon, and the XCAP server determines uniqueness by case-sensitive string comparison. Because each of these attributes contains URIs, and the URI equality rules for their schemes may allow two URIs to be the same even if they differ by case-sensitive string comparison, it is possible that a client will attempt a PUT or DELETE to modify or remove an existing element, and the PUT instead inserts a new element or the DELETE returns an error response.

If the XCAP client cannot determine whether the user's intent is to create or replace, the client SHOULD canonicalize the URI before performing the operation. For a SIP URI, often present in the uri attribute of the entry element, the canonicalization procedure is defined in the document's own section on SIP URI canonicalization. The expectation is that the SIP URIs placed into resource lists documents will usually be of the form sip:user@domain, possibly with a user parameter, and the canonicalization rules work perfectly for these URIs.

For HTTP URIs, a basic canonicalization algorithm is given: if the port in the URI equals the default port, 80 for http URIs, the port is removed; the hostname is converted to all lowercase; and any percent-encoding for characters which do not need to be percent-encoded is removed. A character needs to be percent-encoded when it is not permitted in that part of the URI based on the grammar for that part.

The SIP URI canonicalization procedure has four steps. First, the domain part of the URI is converted into all lowercase, and any tokens such as user, transport or udp are converted to all lowercase. Secondly, any percent-encoding for characters which do not need to be percent-encoded is removed: for example, a SIP URI sip:%6aoe%20smith@example.com is changed to sip:joe%20smith@example.com, because the grammar allows a j to appear in the user part. Thirdly, any URI parameters are reordered so that they appear in lexical order based on parameter name, with the ordering of a character determined by its US-ASCII numerical value and the leftmost character as most significant, which for parameters containing only letters is equivalent to alphabetical ordering. Finally, any header parameters are discarded.

If two URIs, A and B, are functionally equal, meaning equal according to the URI comparison rules in RFC 3261, their canonicalized URIs are equal under case-sensitive string comparison if neither URI contains header parameters, and if one of the URIs contains a URI parameter not defined in RFC 3261, the other does as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Two spellings of the same address would break the edit and delete operations, so both ends put the address into a standard form first: lower case, no unnecessary escapes, parameters in a fixed order.

sections.title: Extending the Formats
sections.content:
Resource-lists and RLS services documents are meant to be extended. An extension takes place by defining a new set of elements in a new namespace, governed by a new schema. Every extension MUST have an appropriate XML namespace assigned to it, and the XML namespace of the extension MUST be different from the namespaces defined in this specification. The extension MUST NOT change the syntax or semantics of the schemas defined in this document, and all XML tags and attributes that are part of the extension MUST be appropriately qualified so as to place them within that namespace.

This specification defines explicit places where new elements or attributes from an extension can be placed. These are indicated in the schemas by the any and anyAttribute elements, and extensions to this specification MUST specify where their elements can be placed within the document.

As a result, a document that contains extensions requires multiple schemas in order to determine its validity: a schema defined in this document, along with those defined by extensions present in the document. Because extensions occur by adding new elements and attributes governed by new schemas, the schemas defined in this document are fixed and would only be changed by a revision to this specification. Such a revision would endeavour to allow documents compliant with the previous schema to remain compliant with the new one, so the schemas defined here do not provide explicit schema versions, as this is not expected to be needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Other documents can add their own elements and attributes, as long as they use their own namespace and put them in the places this document marks as open.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The information contained in rls-services and resource-lists documents is particularly sensitive. It represents the principal set of people with whom a user would like to communicate. As a result, clients SHOULD use TLS when contacting servers in order to fetch this information. The document notes that this does not represent a change in requirement strength from XCAP.

Each application usage leaves the default XCAP authorization policy unchanged, which is that only a user can read, write or modify their own documents. A server can allow privileged users to modify documents they do not own, but establishing and indicating such policies is outside the scope of the document. The index document maintained in the global tree represents sensitive information, as it contains the union of all the information for all users on the server, so its access MUST be restricted to trusted elements within the domain of the server, typically the RLSs that need access to it.
sections.plainLanguage: These files list the people you talk to, so they should travel over an encrypted connection. The global index that merges every user's lists is the most sensitive of all and only the servers that need it should be able to read it.

viz.caption: THE FOUR STEPS OF SIP URI CANONICALIZATION (SECTION 5)

items.title: Lower case the domain and tokens
items.text: The domain part and any tokens such as user, transport or udp become all lowercase.

items.title: Drop needless escapes
items.text: Percent-encoding is removed for characters the grammar allows unescaped, so sip:%6aoe%20smith@example.com becomes sip:joe%20smith@example.com.

items.title: Sort the parameters
items.text: URI parameters are reordered into lexical order by parameter name, smaller US-ASCII values first.

items.title: Discard the headers
items.text: Any header parameters are removed from the URI.
